name: Matrix multiplication

summary: The Matrix multiplication calculator returns C₁₁ (Matrix result (1×1)) from the 76 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Matrix multiplication calculator work?
sections.html:
The Matrix multiplication calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports C₁₁ (Matrix result (1×1)) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of rows (First matrix size), number of columns (First matrix size) and number of rows (Second matrix size)); then you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Matrix multiplication calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

C₁₁=(A₁ × X₁)
C₁₁=(A₂ × Y₁ + (A₁ × X₁))
C₁₁=(A₂ × Y₁ + A₃ × Z₁ + (A₁ × X₁))
C₁₁=((A₁ × X₁))
C₁₂=(A₁ × X₂)
C₁₂=(A₂ × Y₂ + (A₁ × X₂))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Number of rows set to 2, Number of columns set to 2, a₁ = 10 and a₂ = 10. Working through the relationship above gives c₁₁ = 100, c₁₂ = 100, c₁₃ = 100 and c₂₁ = 200.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: c₁₁ = 100, c₁₂ = 100, c₁₃ = 100 and c₂₁ = 200 should be roughly the size you expected from Number of rows set to 2 and Number of columns set to 2.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Matrix multiplication calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Matrix multiplication calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns C₁₁ (Matrix result (1×1)). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Matrix multiplication calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 76 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports c₁₁ = 100. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Matrix multiplication calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
